content: Pregnancy in mammals refers to the reproductive period during which a female carries one or more live offspring from the point of implantation in the uterus through the entire gestational process. This process begins when a fertilized zygote implants into the uterine lining and concludes when the offspring exits the uterus. Fertilization and Implantation During copulation, the male inseminates the female, introducing spermatozoa into the female reproductive tract. Fertilization occurs when a sperm cell successfully merges with an ovum (or multiple ova) in the uterus or fallopian tubes, resulting in the formation of one or more zygotes. In some cases, zygotes can also be created outside the body through in-vitro fertilization. Following fertilization, the zygote undergoes mitotic division, forming an embryo. This embryo, typically consisting of 16 cells at this stage, implants into the endometrium of the uterus. Development After Implantation The embryo develops a central cavity called the blastocoele, around which embryonic cells grow. A flat layer of cells forms on the exterior of this cavity, while the zona pellucida, the protective barrier of the blastocyst, remains unchanged in size. As the cells divide, they become progressively smaller to fit within the structure. This new structure, with a central cavity and surrounding cells, is termed a blastocyst. The blastocyst contains two distinct cell types: an inner cell mass that will develop into the embryo and outer cells that will contribute to the placenta. Within 24 to 48 hours, the zona pellucida ruptures, and the outer cells of the blastocyst secrete enzymes that erode the uterine epithelial lining, creating a site for implantation. Placental Circulation System The outer cells of the blastocyst invade the uterine lining, destroying cells and forming small blood pools that stimulate the development of capillaries. This marks the initial stage of placental formation. The inner cell mass of the blastocyst rapidly divides into two layers: the top layer forms the embryo, occupying the amniotic cavity, while the bottom layer forms a small sac. If cells develop in an abnormal location, an ectopic pregnancy may occur at this stage. A few days later, chorionic villi from the developing placenta anchor the implantation site to the uterus. A network of blood vessels begins to form at the site of the placenta, facilitating nutrient exchange. The small sac within the blastocyst starts producing red blood cells. Over the next 24 hours, connective tissue develops between the placenta and the growing embryo, eventually forming the umbilical cord. Cellular Differentiation A narrow line of cells appears on the surface of the embryo, initiating gastrulation. During this process, the three primary germ layers of the fetus—ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm—develop. The narrow line of cells forms the endoderm and mesoderm, while the ectoderm grows rapidly due to chemical signals from the mesoderm. These three layers give rise to all tissue types in the body. The endoderm forms the linings of the tongue, digestive tract, lungs, bladder, and certain glands. The mesoderm develops into muscle, bone, lymphatic tissue, the interior of the lungs, the heart, and the reproductive and excretory systems. It also forms the spleen and produces blood cells. The ectoderm gives rise to the skin, nails, hair, cornea, linings of the internal and external ear, nose, sinuses, mouth, anus, teeth, pituitary gland, mammary glands, eyes, and the entire nervous system. Approximately 18 days after fertilization, the embryo has developed much of the tissue it will require. It takes on a pear-like shape, with the head region larger than the tail. The nervous system is one of the first organ systems to develop, beginning in a concave area called the neural groove. The circulatory system continues to expand, forming networks that allow blood to flow throughout the embryo. Blood cells are already being produced and circulating through these networks. Secondary blood vessels begin to form around the placenta to supply it with additional nutrients. Blood cells also form within the sac at the center of the embryo, and some cells differentiate into blood vessels. Endocardial cells start forming the myocardium. By approximately 24 days post-fertilization, a primitive S-shaped tubular heart begins to beat, initiating the flow of fluids throughout the embryo.
